# Maternal Mortality, Health Investment & Service Coverage: 8-Country Comparison

## Overview
Four interrelated datasets track maternal mortality outcomes, health spending, skilled birth attendance, and rural-urban disparities across eight low- and middle-income countries (Ethiopia, India, Rwanda, Bangladesh, Nigeria, Cambodia, Peru, Nepal) from 2005 to 2021.

## Data Source

### maternal_mortality_timeseries
- **Fields**: `country` (string, 8 values), `year` (integer, 2005/2009/2013/2017/2021), `mmr` (integer, deaths per 100,000 live births, range 69–946)

Skip to content
Policy Research · Maternal Health

Maternal Mortality & Health Investment

Tracking mortality decline, spending patterns, skilled birth attendance, and rural–urban disparities across eight low- and middle-income countries, 2005–2021.

Countries 8 LMICs
Time Span 2005–2021
Metric Deaths per 100k live births
Source WHO / DHS Methodology
Insight 1 · Trend Over Time

Maternal Mortality Decline & Health Expenditure Trajectory

Each country's MMR decline (solid line) paired with health spending as % of GDP (dashed line). Higher investment periods correlate with faster mortality reductions in most cases.

Countries:
Key finding: Ethiopia declined from 871 to 267 (−69%) and Rwanda from 720 to 203 (−72%) — the steepest sustained falls — both during periods of rising health expenditure. Nigeria's persistently low spending (~3.4% GDP) tracks its slow progress.
Insight 2 · Rural–Urban Disparity

Rural vs. Urban Maternal Mortality (~2019–2021)

The gap between rural and urban mortality reveals how geography creates inequity. Countries are ranked by rural MMR magnitude.

Starkest gap: Nigeria rural 860 vs. urban 350 — a 2.5× multiplier. Peru shows the smallest absolute gap (rural 125, urban 38) but still a 3.3× ratio. Closing the rural–urban divide is critical for equitable progress.
Insight 3 · Midwife Coverage

Skilled Birth Attendant Coverage: Early vs. Recent Period

Change in percentage of births attended by skilled personnel between 2008–2012 and 2018–2021. Countries ordered by 2021 MMR — those with highest coverage tend to have lowest mortality.

Ethiopia's leap: From just 10% to 50% coverage — the largest absolute gain (+40 pp). Rwanda reached 91% and Peru 95%. Nigeria's 5 pp gain (38→43%) helps explain its stalled mortality decline.
Insight 4 · Steepest Declines

Countries with Fastest Maternal Mortality Reduction (2005→2021)

Countries ranked by absolute MMR reduction over 16 years — spotlighting the strongest performers against the slowest movers.

Rwanda and Ethiopia lead with reductions of 517 and 604 deaths per 100k respectively. Nigeria — despite the second-highest starting point — reduced by only 325 over the same period and remains the highest-mortality country in 2021.
Insight 5 · Spending–Mortality Relationship

Health Expenditure (% GDP) vs. Maternal Mortality — All Countries & Time Points

Each point represents one country at one time point (40 observations). Point size reflects the year (larger = more recent). The relationship reveals a general pattern: higher spending correlates with lower mortality, though structural factors beyond spending matter.

Bubble size = year (larger = more recent); each country is a distinct color
Pattern: Points cluster in two bands — countries spending >5% of GDP tend to have lower MMR trajectories. However, Bangladesh achieves strong improvements despite lower spending (~2.6%), while Nigeria spends ~3.4% with persistently high mortality — indicating governance and service delivery quality matter as much as raw expenditure.

Data notes: MMR figures are modeled estimates aligned with WHO/UNICEF methodology. Rural–urban splits are approximate estimates for ~2019–2021. Skilled birth attendant percentages are drawn from Demographic and Health Surveys. Cambodia's 2021 MMR reflects a reporting methodology change. Health expenditure includes public and private spending.
